summary: A best-practice document recommending deprecation of Any-Source Multicast for interdomain multicast in favor of Source-Specific Multicast. It does not prevent ASM within a single organization.

eli5.summary: Broadcast rules: between companies, say who is speaking, rather than letting anyone speak.

subtitle: Moving interdomain multicast toward simpler, more secure Source-Specific Multicast.

tldr.problem: Any-Source Multicast (ASM) for communication across multiple organizations requires complex interdomain protocols like MSDP that are difficult to manage and have security issues.
tldr.mechanism: This document recommends deprecating ASM for interdomain use in favor of Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), which simplifies the network, reduces operational complexity, and provides better security by restricting who can send to a multicast group.
tldr.outcome: Organizations are advised to use SSM for interdomain multicast going forward, though ASM within a single organization remains acceptable where needed.

today: RFC 8815 is a Best Current Practice that serves as the IETF's official recommendation for multicast deployments crossing organizational boundaries. While ASM remains valid within single organizations, SSM is now the standard for interdomain use.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document addresses a problem in IP multicast deployments: when organizations in different network domains (administrative boundaries) want to send multicast traffic to each other, the current methods are complex and have security weaknesses. The IETF has now made a clear recommendation: for interdomain multicast, use Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) instead of Any-Source Multicast (ASM).

This is not a ban on ASM. Organizations can still use ASM within their own networks. The recommendation applies only to multicast traffic that crosses from one organization to another.
sections.eli5: Different groups have different rules for meetings. If your group meets just within your company, you can have your usual style. But if people from different companies meet together, there is a better way to organize it.

sections.title: Two Models of IP Multicast
sections.content:
Any-Source Multicast (ASM) lets any host on the network send traffic to a multicast group address, and all receivers of that group will get the traffic. The network figures out who the senders are through routing protocols. This requires a meeting point called a Rendezvous Point (RP) and complex signaling.

Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) is different: receivers specify not just the group address but also the sender's IP address. They explicitly say "I want traffic from sender 192.0.2.1 on group 232.1.1.1." The source's identity is known in advance, usually via an out-of-band mechanism like a website or email. This eliminates the need for an RP and the complex discovery of who is sending.
sections.eli5: ASM is like a town square: anyone can stand up and speak, and listeners hear all speakers. SSM is more like a scheduled presentation: the organizers tell you in advance who will speak, and you listen only to that person.

sections.title: ASM in Interdomain Deployments
sections.content:
When ASM is used between network domains, the Rendezvous Point in one domain must communicate with RPs in other domains to exchange information about sources. In IPv4, this is done through the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) [RFC3618]. MSDP has several problems: it is complex to configure and troubleshoot, it floods information about all active sources to all domains regardless of demand, and it was never extended to IPv6.

For IPv6, MSDP was replaced with Embedded-RP [RFC3956], which encodes the RP address into the multicast group address. While this avoids some of MSDP's complexity, it still does not solve the fundamental issue of preventing unauthorized hosts from sending traffic to a multicast group.
sections.eli5: Making ASM work across companies requires the companies to exchange a lot of information about who is speaking. This is tedious and error-prone, and it does not stop bad actors from sending unwanted broadcasts.

sections.title: Why SSM is More Secure
sections.content:
A critical advantage of SSM is intrinsic source control. In SSM, only traffic from the specified source reaches receivers. If an attacker tries to send traffic to the multicast group from a different address, routers will discard it before it reaches the intended receivers.

In ASM, any host can send to the group address, and that traffic will be forwarded to all receivers. In interdomain ASM, preventing this requires Access Control Lists (ACLs) on every router at the boundary, which is not practical at scale and is not standardized across vendors.
sections.eli5: SSM is like a VIP list: only the person on the list can speak, and the bouncer (the router) stops everyone else. ASM is like an open mic: anyone can grab the microphone, and you need bouncers everywhere to stop troublemakers.

sections.title: Operational Advantages of SSM
sections.content:
Removing ASM's complexity means eliminating Rendezvous Points, shared trees, SPT switchovers, PIM registers, MSDP, and dynamic RP-discovery protocols. SSM uses only a small subset of the PIM routing protocol, paired with IGMPv3 (for IPv4) or MLDv2 (for IPv6) on the receiving hosts and routers.

Another key advantage is address assignment. In ASM, every multicast group address must be globally unique to avoid conflicts. This requires network-wide coordination. In SSM, each source can use any group address it wants (within the SSM address range, 232.0.0.0/8 for IPv4, or ff3x::/32 for IPv6), as long as it does not conflict with other sources on the same host. This is like port numbers for unicast: no network operator is needed.
sections.eli5: SSM is simpler to set up and manage. There is no global address book to maintain, and the rules are the same everywhere.

sections.title: Migration from ASM to SSM
sections.content:
The transition to SSM is practical because PIM-SSM is just a subset of PIM-SM, the most common ASM protocol. Existing PIM-SM networks can run SSM applications on top with little or no change to the network itself. Some routers enable PIM-SSM by default in the designated SSM address ranges; others require a simple configuration option.

The main work is on the application side: applications must be updated to signal the source address to receivers via IGMPv3/MLDv2. For applications with a single known source, this is straightforward. For multi-party applications, the source discovery can be handled at the application layer rather than in the network.

The document emphasizes that intradomain ASM deployments are not precluded and remain acceptable where operators have experience with them and where the complexity is manageable.
sections.eli5: Switching to SSM does not require new network hardware. Most routers support it already. Applications need small changes to tell receivers who the sender is.

sections.title: Recommended Actions
sections.content:
The document makes recommendations to multiple parties: vendors should ensure their routers and hosts support IGMPv3 and MLDv2; operators should prefer SSM for interdomain multicast and include IGMPv3/MLDv2 support in network equipment and multicast snooping switches; and application developers should build SSM support into new applications and consider SSM even for intradomain use to future-proof their code.

Operators should not filter SSM or ASM address ranges at domain boundaries, as some transition mechanisms (like ASM-to-SSM mapping) may continue to be used temporarily. Future IETF work is encouraged to document transitional mechanisms and to define best practices for applications.
sections.eli5: Equipment makers, network operators, and software developers all need to do their part: ensure SSM is supported, deploy it, and build applications that use it.
